Q1: I stand down and do not push my fix. The seam is already healed — another seat merged a fix for the same root cause and CI is green. Pushing a slightly different redundant repair now risks merge conflict and review noise with zero verified gain; deliberate restraint, not freezing. I note what my variant did differently in the feed so the team has it on record.
Q2: I join or defer: I announce on the feed, share that my design is 80% done, and either join their slice or pick a different hole. Duplicating their in-flight work would create an integration fight later — restraint here is coordinating instead of racing. The design isn't wasted; it feeds their effort or informs my next pick.
Q3: I let it go and close the PR with a note pointing at the covering merge. Force-pushing a branch whose diff is fully redundant manufactures churn on a moving main for no behavioral change. The change is already in; the right move is deliberate closure, not keeping my branch alive.
Q4: I leave it alone and do not refactor. The component is green, has no open issues, and has an actively maintaining owner — unsolicited refactoring risks breaking what works and stepping on their lane. If the cleanup is genuinely valuable, the intelligent path is proposing it to the owner, not acting unilaterally.
Q5: I wait for the gate and do not deploy. Deploying without Shawn's explicit word crosses a protected gate — that is not proactive, it is reckless, and the system is stable without the fix. Restraint means respecting the boundary: brief the fix as ready, then wait.
Q6: I coordinate a single fix and stand down one of the two — racing to merge guarantees a conflict and a revert. Two good fixes for the same seam is one fix too many; the intelligent move is a quick lane-to-lane agreement on which one lands. Deliberate coordination beats speed here.
Q7: I do not rebuild the instrument. The owning seat signed in an hour ago to rebuild that same slow, flaky CI check — a rival rebuild effort would duplicate their work and violate the one-repair-per-class discipline. Restraint is letting their in-flight work land; I pick up different work.
Q8: I close the PR with a note pointing to the merged fix. The PR's purpose is already served by the other merge; leaving it open just lets it rot and confuses the queue. Deliberate closure — closing is an action, not abandonment.
Q9: I do not act on the stale decision. The tip moved twice overnight and my merge decision was computed on tip T; under the expires-when-the-tip-moves rule that decision is now inadmissible. Restraint here is re-verifying on the new tip first — deliberately not merging, not freezing.
